Commentary.Commentary: High stakes in Manchester - A crunch game awaits in Group 1 at Old Trafford as South Africa take on India in a clash that could have a major bearing on the race to the semifinals. The stakes are particularly high for South Africa, who have already suffered a defeat to Australia and can ill afford another loss. India, meanwhile, have won their opening two games and, with South Africa one of the sides expected to challenge them for a semifinal spot, a victory here would put them in a strong position to reach the last four. Openers lead the way - Coming into the tournament, much was said about India's reliance on their opening pair, and so far, the duo has delivered. Smriti Mandhana has produced back-to-back fifties, while Shafali Verma returned to form with a half-century against the Netherlands. That knock will do her confidence a world of good after a lean run in the England series leading into the World Cup and a quiet set of warm-up matches. What India do with the make-up of their middle order remains to be seen. Bharti Fulmali featured in the opening game against Pakistan before making way for Yastika Bhatia against the Netherlands. Whether chopping and changing in that role helps either player settle into the tournament remains open to debate. Questions with the ball - India's powerplay returns remain a concern. Pakistan raced to 52/1, and the Netherlands reached 39/1, with the new-ball attack struggling to make early inroads. As a result, much of the burden has fallen on Deepti Sharma and Sree Charani to provide breakthroughs through the middle overs. The Women in Blue have also been dealt a blow with Shreyanka Patil ruled out of the remainder of the tournament after suffering an ankle ligament injury in the previous game. It continues a frustrating run with injuries for the off-spinner, who also missed the 2024 edition with a broken finger. Leg-spinner Prema Rawat has been drafted in as her replacement. With tougher assignments against South Africa and Australia still to come, India will need to sharpen up in the field and find a way to be more effective with the new ball if they are to cement their place in the semifinals. Looking for sharper execution - South Africa suffered a heavy defeat to Australia and then missed an opportunity to significantly boost their net run rate against Pakistan. While they eventually got over the line, it was far from convincing. Pakistan recovered from 50/8 to post 126, with South Africa conceding 38 runs in the final three overs. Their death bowling is one area they will be keen to tighten up heading into a game of such importance. They will bank on early strikes from the experienced and trusted new-ball pairing of Marizanne Kapp and Shabnim Ismail. South Africa know that dismissing India's openers early could go a long way towards shaping the contest. The batting backbone - Sune Luus has endured a string of low scores, both in the lead-up to the World Cup and in the opening two games of the tournament. Tazmin Brits is waiting in the wings, but Luus earned plenty of credit during the home T20I series against India earlier this year, averaging 49.25 and registering a pair of half-centuries. Then there is Laura Wolvaardt, who enjoys facing India. South Africa's captain has scored more T20I runs against India than against any other opposition. The Proteas will look towards Wolvaardt, Kapp and Nadine De Klerk, while hoping for another strong contribution from the young Annerie Dercksen, who continues to grow in stature with every opportunity. Team form (Last 5 completed T20Is, recent first) - IND-W - WWLLW | SA-W - WLWLW. Familiar foes, new stage - Earlier this year, these two sides met in South Africa, where the Proteas Women handed India a 4-1 drubbing. Despite the two teams having faced each other regularly in recent years, this will be their first meeting at a Women's T20 World Cup. Conditions in focus - Old Trafford has produced good batting surfaces in this tournament, with both matches at the venue seeing scores in excess of 160. While the batters have generally enjoyed the conditions, there has also been enough assistance for the seamers with the new ball. With both sides boasting quality with both bat and ball, the ingredients are in place for a highly competitive encounter.
